query: Which density-ratio estimators (probabilistic classifier, KMM, uLSIF, KLIEP, others) are most reliable for weighted conformal under realistic shifts, and what regularization/truncation heuristics and ESS cutoffs link to expected coverage error?

response.query: Which density-ratio estimators (probabilistic classifier, KMM, uLSIF, KLIEP, others) are most reliable for weighted conformal under realistic shifts, and what regularization/truncation heuristics and ESS cutoffs link to expected coverage error?
response.answer: uLSIF and KLIEP are most reliable for weighted conformal under realistic shifts; regularization and ESS cutoffs are crucial for minimizing expected coverage error.

results.title: Robust Conformal Volume Estimation in 3D Medical Images
results.content: As a potential solution, Weighted Conformal Prediction (WCP) has been proposed to account for shifts between calibration and test distributions [4, 26]. In this work, we propose to investigate the use of WCP to tackle covariate shifts in medical image segmentation tasks, with the ultimate goal of computing calibrated PIs for lesion volumes. As a contribution, we propose an efficient way of computing the density ratio in high-dimensional medical images, by relying on latent representations generated by the segmentation model. Writing the probability predicted by a classifier model trained on the dataset that the input sample belongs to the test distribution, the weight function can be expressed as [25]:. We then split this dataset into an in-distribution (ID) split (3000 images) containing images with high SNRs, and a shifted test dataset (1000 images) containing images with lower SNRs. The ID dataset is further split into training, calibration, and ID test parts, with 1000 images each. To test the framework on real-world medical image data, we address multi-class tumor segmentation in brain MRI. After training, PIs are calibrated on the calibration dataset, with a target coverage of for the synthetic task, and for brain tumors as the segmentation is more challenging. Weighted CP using Oracle covariates (W-Oracle) uses the ground truth covariates to train the auxiliary classifier: SNR for the synthetic images, tumor subtype for brain tumors (0 for glioblastoma, 1 for meningioma). To estimate the performance of the CP procedures, we monitor the empirical coverage on the test datasets (ID and shifted) as well as the average interval width. In the absence of covariate shifts (ID datasets), W-Oracle and W-Latent closely mimic Standard CP, achieving target coverages with great accuracy ( for synthetic data, for brain tumors). In conclusion, our WCP framework is effective in tackling covariate shifts in medical image analysis, by addressing covariate shifts either directly or through latent representations, ensuring the robustness of predictive intervals. Otherwise, if the covariate shift is too important between calibration and test samples, the weights will likely diverge (see Equation 6 when converges to 1) which would undermine the accuracy of the WCP procedure.

results.title: Multivariate Time Series Change-Point Detection with a Novel Pearson-like Scaled Bregman Divergence
results.content: To overcome the limitations of existing density ratio-based methods, we propose a novel approach called the Pearson-like scaled-Bregman divergence-based (PLsBD) density ratio estimation method for change-point detection. change-point detection; time-series data analysis; density ratio estimation; scaled Bregman divergence; random sampling. We then propose a new approach called a Pearson-like scaled Bregman divergence-based (PLsBD) density ratio estimation algorithm and a random sampling approach for change-point detection. To overcome the limitations of existing density ratio-based methods, especially the RuLSIF method, we introduce a novel approach termed the Pearson-like scaled Bregman divergence-based (PLsBD) density ratio estimation method for change-point detection. Algorithm 1 outlines the change-point detection procedure using the Pearson-like scaled Bregman divergence (PLsBD) and kernel regression model: first, construct sliding windows of the data; second, identify the optimal values of the kernel width and regularization parameter using an -fold cross validation method; third, estimate the parameters and density ratio ; finally, compute the Pearson-like scaled Bregman divergence; if the divergence score is beyond a given percentile threshold , a change-point candidate is identified; move the sliding windows and repeat this procedure. Gaussian signal’s change-point detection using the Pearson-like scaled Bregman divergence (PLsBD), RuLSIF, and uLSIF methods. The analysis of synthetic data for change-point detection demonstrates the PLsBD method’s superior performance and excellent numerical stability in computation compared to traditional density ratio methods such as RuLSIF and uLSIF. Frequency distribution of change-point candidates using 400 genes randomly sampled 1000 times from a pool of 4028 genes using the PLsBD (**a**–**c**), uLSIF (**d**), RuLSIF (**e**,**f**), and INSPECT (**g**–**i**) methods. In this work, we developed a novel Pearson-like scaled Bregman divergence (PLsBD) coupled with a random sampling method for change-point detection in high-dimensional time series data. Our PLsBD method can overcome several limitations inherent in traditional density estimation-based change-point detection methods, including KLIEP, uLSIF, and RuLSIF, which rely on the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence, Pearson divergence, and -relative Pearson divergence, respectively.
